blocks.text: 1. L2 Regularization
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445071268-951777262.png

L1 Regularization, the previous topic, introduced penalizing the sum of absolute weight values, producing genuinely sparse, mostly-zero weights. L2 Regularization is a closely related technique with a genuinely different mathematical shape.

Instead of penalizing the sum of absolute weight values, it penalizes the sum of squared weights, a small mathematical change with genuinely significant, distinctive consequences covered throughout this topic.
2. The Core Idea
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445071268-638763250.png

This connects back to any loss function already covered in the Loss Functions module. L2 Regularization adds a new term to that existing loss: the sum of the squares of every single weight in the network.

Larger weights now contribute a genuinely much larger penalty, since squaring amplifies size considerably more than the plain absolute value already covered in L1 Regularization, meaning L2 punishes genuinely large individual weights especially aggressively.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Component","Role"],"rows":[["Original loss","Measures prediction error, exactly as already covered in Loss Functions"],["L2 penalty","The sum of squared weight values, added on top"]]}

blocks.text: 3. The Core Mathematical Difference From L1

blocks.alt: The Core Mathematical Difference From L1
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445071268-979330023.png

This connects directly back to L1 Regularization's own sharp corner at zero, already covered as a genuine computational consideration in that topic. Squaring, by contrast, is smooth everywhere, with no sharp corner at zero at all.

Because of this smoothness, weights shrink toward zero under L2 Regularization but almost never reach exactly zero, a genuinely important, distinctive contrast with L1's own sparsity-inducing behavior already covered in the previous topic.
4. Shrinkage, Not Sparsity
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445071269-277612104.png

This connects back to the sparsity property already covered in L1 Regularization, where some weights get driven all the way to exactly zero. L2 Regularization instead produces what is genuinely called shrinkage.

Every weight gets genuinely smaller under L2 Regularization, but none typically hit exactly zero, a fundamentally different outcome than L1's own sparse, mostly-zero weight pattern already covered in the previous topic.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This means L2 Regularization does not perform the automatic feature selection already covered as L1's own distinctive strength. Every input keeps at least some small influence on the model's final predictions.

blocks.text: 5. The Weight Decay Connection
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445071269-362139807.png

A genuinely important practical connection: in gradient-based training, already covered throughout the Backpropagation & Optimization module, L2's penalty gradient turns out to be directly proportional to the weight itself.

This is exactly why L2 Regularization is also commonly called Weight Decay, a term covered in its own upcoming topic later in this module, since the practical effect during each training update genuinely looks like every weight decaying slightly toward zero.
6. The Regularization Strength

This uses the same lambda hyperparameter already covered in L1 Regularization. A larger lambda produces stronger shrinkage, pulling weights genuinely closer to zero, following the same pattern already covered for L1.
A smaller lambda produces weaker shrinkage instead, keeping training closer to plain, unregularized behavior, tunable through the same Hyperparameter Tuning process covered later in this course.
7. Connecting Back to Bias-Variance

This connects back to the Bias-Variance Tradeoff, already covered in its own dedicated topic. L2 Regularization deliberately increases bias slightly, since it constrains the model away from perfectly fitting the training data.

This happens in direct exchange for a genuinely larger reduction in variance, exactly the same deliberate tradeoff already covered for L1 Regularization, just achieved through this topic's own distinctive shrinkage mechanism rather than sparsity.
8. A Genuine Advantage With Correlated Features

blocks.alt: A Genuine Advantage With Correlated Features
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445071269-159145141.png
A genuine, practical advantage over L1 Regularization emerges when several input features are genuinely correlated with each other, a common, real situation in many practical datasets.

L2 tends to spread weight evenly across genuinely correlated features, rather than arbitrarily zeroing some out the way L1's own sparsity property, already covered in the previous topic, tends to do in this exact situation.
9. Recognizing When L2 Regularization Is Genuinely The Default

blocks.alt: Recognizing When L2 Regularization Is Genuinely The Default
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445071269-191770228.png

Most inputs being genuinely believed to matter, at least somewhat, is a direct case for L2 Regularization, since its shrinkage, already covered throughout this topic, keeps every input's influence without eliminating any entirely.

Correlated input features being genuinely present is another genuine case, since its robustness to correlated features, already covered in the previous section, spreads weight more evenly than L1's own arbitrary zeroing behavior.

blocks.text: 10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates L2 Regularization's shrinkage property, contrasting it against L1 Regularization's sparsity property on the very same, genuinely correlated data.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge, Lasso  # Ridge is scikit-learn's name for L2-regularized linear regression

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
n_samples, n_features = 200, 10
base = rng.normal(size=(n_samples, 1))

# Features 0 and 1 are genuinely, strongly correlated with each other
X = np.hstack([base + rng.normal(scale=0.1, size=(n_samples, 1)),
                base + rng.normal(scale=0.1, size=(n_samples, 1)),
                rng.normal(size=(n_samples, n_features - 2))])

true_weights = np.zeros(n_features)
true_weights[0] = 2.0
true_weights[1] = 2.0
y = X @ true_weights + rng.normal(scale=0.5, size=n_samples)

ridge = Ridge(alpha=1.0)  # L2 Regularization, already covered throughout this topic
lasso = Lasso(alpha=0.1)  # L1 Regularization, already covered in the previous topic

ridge.fit(X, y)
lasso.fit(X, y)

print("Feature 0 and Feature 1 are genuinely correlated with each other:")
print(f"  Ridge (L2) weights: {ridge.coef_[0]:.3f}, {ridge.coef_[1]:.3f} (spread evenly, as covered in this topic)")
print(f"  Lasso (L1) weights: {lasso.coef_[0]:.3f}, {lasso.coef_[1]:.3f} (often arbitrarily favors one)")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example typically shows Ridge (L2) assigning genuinely similar weight to both correlated features, while Lasso (L1) often assigns most of the weight to just one of them, exactly the contrast already covered in this topic.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: L2 Regularization adds a penalty to the loss based on the sum of squared weight values.
Squaring amplifies size, so genuinely large weights get punished especially aggressively.
Its smooth penalty shape produces shrinkage, not sparsity: weights get smaller but rarely hit exactly zero.
It does not perform automatic feature selection the way L1 Regularization does.
Its penalty gradient being proportional to the weight itself is why it is also called Weight Decay.
Lambda, the same regularization strength hyperparameter from L1, controls how aggressively weights shrink.
It deliberately trades a small amount of increased bias for a genuinely larger reduction in variance.
It handles genuinely correlated features more gracefully than L1, spreading weight evenly rather than zeroing arbitrarily.
Next up: Dropout, a genuinely different regularization approach that works by randomly disabling neurons during training rather than penalizing weights at all.
